title: Teaching robots to say no
text: One of the hardest problems in robotics is not movement {{1}} judgement. A household robot must decide not only how to carry out tasks but {{2}} whether to carry them out at all. Demand a cup of tea and a well-designed robot will comply; demand {{3}} absurd a hundred times, and it should perhaps object. Researchers in Bristol have programmed a robot to refuse politely when requests become unreasonable, {{4}} on factors such as repetition and safety. The robot explains {{5}} it is refusing, which users report makes refusal far less annoying. The team stresses {{6}} the goal is not stubbornness but cooperation: {{7}} machines that push back occasionally are easier to trust than machines that never do. Early trials suggest people adjust quickly, often moderating their demands {{8}} their own accord.

gaps.explanation: 'not A but B' — contrast of nouns.
'not only…but also' — the 'also' completes the pair.
'demand it' — the same request; pronoun refers to the tea demand.
'draw on' = use as a basis; participle clause.
Subject noun repeated in apposition: machines that push back are easier to trust.
'of their own accord' = voluntarily — fixed phrase.
